extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian ethics; philosophy students and ethicists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Aristotle's account of moral virtues and their corresponding excesses and defects (e.g., liberality, magnificence, great-mindedness, meekness, tact/truthfulness, social intercourse) as presented in the Nicomachean Ethics. Focus is on the definitional criteria, examples, and anti-patterns Aristotle gives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality and Stinginess
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality concerns proper giving and receiving of wealth; Stinginess is its contrary, manifesting either as deficiency in giving or excessive willingness to receive from base sources. "Stinginess called the contrary of Liberality" and is more common than prodigality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes those "deficient in giving" (sparing, close-fisted, niggards) from those "Stingy in respect of receiving" who accept anything from any source (usurers, brothel-keepers, those who gain by base means). Examples of base-gaining: usurers, dicer, bath-plunderer, robber — all submit to disgrace for the sake of gain. Guidance: avoid receiving from improper sources or in improper amounts; giving should be appropriate to what one ought to give. Note: Stinginess is judged a greater evil than Prodigality and is a common human error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue with Wealth as its object-matter but limited to large-scale or expensive expenditures; "fitting expense on a large scale" — doing great things in a fitting and tasteful manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnificence applies where expenditure is large (e.g., equipping/commanding a trireme vs giving a public spectacle). The magnificent person spends greatly but fittingly: work must be proportionate to expense and to the doer, and motives should be honourable. Typical honourable expenditures: dedicatory offerings to the gods, temple furnishings, sacrifices, public spectacles, fitting out a trireme, public feasts, marriage expenses, receiving/despatching strangers, gifts and repaying gifts. Consider rank and means: expenditure must be proportionate to the individual's wealth and station (a poor man attempting magnificence is a fool). Prefer beauty and appropriateness over mere cheapness; excessive calculation is mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgar Profusion (excess of Magnificence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The excess contrary to Magnificence where one "spends improperly" and shows off in improper objects or manner; lavishes in small matters to display wealth rather than to secure what is honourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's examples: giving a club a feast fit for a wedding, furnishing actors with purple inappropriately, spending little where one ought to spend much and much where one ought to spend little. This vice aims at display and admiration rather than fitting, honourable ends. The mean and the deficiency (Meanness) are both faulty; Vulgar Profusion is not simply large expense but misapplied, tasteless expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great-mindedness (Megalopsychia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great-mindedness implies valuing oneself highly and justly — "he is thought to be Great-minded who values himself highly and at the same time justly"; its special object-matter is honour (great things).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The great-minded man estimates his worth at its true, high rate and thus bears himself properly with respect to honour and dishonour (accepts honour from worthy sources, despises trivial praise). He must also be a genuinely good person — greatness of soul presupposes moral goodness. Traits: asks favours reluctantly, performs services readily, is lofty toward the very great, affable toward the middle, slow and deliberate in motion and speech, not easily flattered, does not bear malice, prefers to give than to receive, will incur great risks for worthy ends. Anti-patterns: Vain man (values himself without grounds), Small-minded man (underestimates his deserts). Great-mindedness ennobles the other virtues and is hard to achieve because it requires thorough goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vainness and Small-mindedness (excess and defect of Great-mindedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vainness: valuing oneself unduly (excess); Small-mindedness: estimating oneself below true worth (defect). Both are errors relative to Great-mindedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vain persons display themselves by dress, carriage, talking of good circumstances, and attempt honourable acts beyond their merit; often foolish and self-ignorant. Small-minded persons, though perhaps truly worthy, fail to grasp their deserts and thus refrain from honourable actions; this self-undervaluation regulates aims and is detrimental. Small-mindedness is more common and worse relative to Great-mindedness according to Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate love of Honour (Lover of Honour vs Ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mean regarding the pursuit of Honour distinct from Great-mindedness: one can aim at honour more or less than is right, or from improper sources; the mean state (praiseworthy) properly values honour for noble ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lover of Honour as praise-worthy aims for honour appropriately (manly, loving what is noble). The excess is analogous to Ambition — aiming at honour more than one ought or from wrong motives; the defect is a lack of desire for honour even when deserved. The mean lacks a special proper name but is to be held: pursue honour for noble causes, from right sources, and in the right measure. Contextual judgement is often required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meekness (regulating Anger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meekness is the mean with Anger as its object: being angry at what and with whom one ought, and in right manner, at right time, and for proper length of time — the appropriately regulated anger is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect: Angerlessness (not angry when one ought to be) — seen as slavish or lacking perception. Excesses include: Passionate (soon angry, excessive but quickly cooled), Choleric (constantly vehement), Bitter-tempered (repress anger and long-lasting resentment), Cross-grained (anger at wrong objects, excessive duration, not appeased without vengeance). Aristotle notes difficulty in fixing precise bounds; slight departures are less blameworthy than great ones; the mean is determined by particulars and moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-intercourse mean (between Over-Complaisant and Cross/Contentious)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean in social conduct: not always agreeing to give pleasure nor always opposing; one "will let pass what he ought as he ought, and also will object in like manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-Complaisant: agrees to everything solely to give pleasure and never opposes (blameable). Cross and Contentious: opposes all and cares not to give pleasure (blameable). The mean — akin to Friendship — acts from propriety, aims to avoid giving pain and contribute to pleasure but always with regard to what is noble and expedient, regulating behavior by the relation and rank of persons. Flatterer is the Over-Complaisant motivated by profit. Sometimes inflicting little pain is justified for consequent greater pleasure; responses vary with the person's station and the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness (Plain-matter-of-fact) vs Exaggeration and Reserve
rubrics_metrics.description: The Truthful man is the mean in claims about himself and conduct: admits what belongs to him neither greater nor less than the truth. Exaggerator and Reserved are the extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerator (Braggart): lays claim to credit not his, or overstates accomplishments — blameworthy, especially when for gain. Braggarts may do so for glory or pecuniary advantage. Reserved: depreciates his own qualities; can appear refined in moderation but may also be excessive in denying what is plainly his. Truthfulness in indifferent matters tends to reflect and promote goodness; falsehood is base. Distinctions: some false claims are knavish (for gain), others foolish (for pleasure in falsehood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity and Tact (mean between Buffoonish and Clownish)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mean in jocularity: a gentlemanly jocularity or "Tact/Easy Pleasantry" that fits what is becoming to say and hear; extremes are Buffoon (excess) and Clownish/Stern (defect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buffoons and the Vulgar catch at the ridiculous at any cost, spare neither themselves nor others, and aim only to raise laughter even by pain or indecency. Clownish persons refuse to jest and are savage toward those who do. The tactful jest aims to avoid wounding the object, may give pleasure, and is appropriate to the education and station of speaker and listeners. Aristotle notes differences between cultivated (innuendo-based) and vulgar (obscene) humour (Old vs New Comedy). Some jesting is legally or morally forbidden; the refined man is a law to himself in what he will say and hear.
